activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
Ariana sat in the guidance counsellor's office with her hands curled in her lap, waiting for Mrs. Okafor to finish writing. She had signed up for this meeting on the voluntary sign-up sheet outside the door, mostly because her stomach had been doing flips all week and she wanted to know why. The posters on the wall said words like anxiety and coping in big calm letters, and she kept reading them while she waited.

"So," said Mrs. Okafor, "the recital is Friday, and your note says the nerves feel huge."

"They feel like they're going to knock me over," Ariana said. "My hands get cold. My heart pounds. Last year I messed up the whole middle of my piece." She had been thinking about it in class, in bed, even at breakfast, and she was starting to wonder if the nerves themselves were the problem, or something else hiding behind them.

Mrs. Okafor slid a paper across the desk. "Stress is the body's response to a demand or a challenge," she said. "People talk about it like it's always bad, but it isn't." Then she leaned back. "That's all I'm going to tell you. What you do with it is yours."

Ariana frowned at the paper. A response to a challenge. So the pounding heart wasn't just noise; it was her body answering the recital. But answer doing what? On Wednesday she decided to run a test on herself. She had a practice performance in music class, and instead of trying to make the nerves evaporate, she let them be there and paid attention to what happened. When her heart started pounding, she noticed something strange: she could hear every note more sharply. The page looked clearer. She caught a mistake in measure twelve before her fingers made it. When she got nervous on the bus, by contrast, with nothing to focus on, the same feeling just rattled around uselessly.

"So the nerves help only when there's something to aim at," she told Mrs. Okafor on Friday morning. "Like a race. My body is getting me ready to play, not to fall apart." They worked out a plan together, a kind of treaty between Ariana and her own pounding heart: she wouldn't fight it, and she wouldn't let it tell her to skip the recital either. She also set a boundary with her cousin, who kept texting "are you nervous yet" every hour; she asked him to stop until after the show. That was her coping plan, and she carried it down the hallway to the auditorium.

Backstage, her heart thundered. Ariana took her seat at the piano, spread her cold fingers over the keys, and thought, there you are. Then she began to play.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The message appeared in the group chat at 4:32 on Tuesday, right between a photo of Marcus's new bike and three rocket emojis from Priya. It was from Ben: "Guys my grandpa signed my birthday card all weird. He wrote Kovacs Peter. He's losing it maybe?" Aaron stared at the screen. His own last name came after his first name, and so did everyone else's he could think of, except the kids in his class whose families were from China and Japan and Korea. Wei Chen. Sato Kenji. He had never thought about it as a rule before, but there it was, a pattern he could see once he looked.

He typed back: "Wait what's his name usually?" Ben answered: "Peter Kovacs. Like always." Aaron pulled up another chat, the one with his friend Dae, whose parents ran the corner market. "Question," Aaron wrote. "In Korean, does the family name go first?" The reply came fast: "Yeah. Mine's Kim Dae. You just never noticed." Aaron sat back. A test began to form in his mind. If Ben's grandpa wrote the family name first, then maybe he was not confused at all. Maybe Hungarian names worked that way too.

"Ben, ask your grandpa if he meant to do that," Aaron typed. Two long minutes passed, with only a random mushroom meme from Priya filling the silence. Then Ben sent a voice note. In it you could hear an older voice in the background, firm and cheerful: "In Hungarian, the family name comes first. Like the Chinese, the Japanese, the Koreans." Ben came back on, laughing a little. "He says I should decompose my own name and figure out which half is which. Also he says if I eat my vegetables it will strengthen my constitution. He says that a lot."

Aaron smiled and typed, "Tell him some of us already knew that. Well, kind of." Ben sent back a picture of the card, the ink neat and sure, the family name sitting proudly in front. "Grandpa says happy birthday to the whole chat," Ben added. Priya sent six rocket emojis. Marcus wrote, "Best card in the thread." Aaron saved the picture to his phone.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
story:
Jade sat on her bedroom floor with her shoes off, pressing her heel against the pencil mark she had drawn on the wall two weeks ago. Her sneakers had started pinching at school, so she had marked the wall to check something, and now she leaned forward and squinted. The mark had moved. Not by much, but by enough.

"Mom says shoes are expensive," her little brother Denny said from the doorway, holding his own sneakers, which were also tight. He was nine and had worn the same shoes all year. "I only got new ones in September."

"That's the weird part," Jade said. She pulled out a notebook and wrote down what she knew. Denny had needed new shoes in September, and now in March his toes were pushing the ends again, even though his jeans from September still fit fine. Her own shoes pinched too, and her sleeves still reached her wrists. She tapped the pencil against her chin. Feet and hands first, then everything else. Maybe that was the order.

"How do you know?" Denny asked, doubtful. He came in and sat on her bed, swinging his legs.

"I don't know yet. That's why I'm testing it." She held up her hand against Denny's. "Look. Yours are almost as big as mine now. If it's really hands and feet first, your hands should be big too, even though you're little." Denny spread his fingers, and Jade compared them to her own palm. His fingers reached her knuckles. Last summer they had only reached her first finger joints. She wrote that down too.

"There's a chart in my science binder," she said, jumping up. She carried the binder, heavy with a year of notes, across the room and let it drop onto the bed with a thump that made Denny laugh. She flipped through until she found the page about growing. She read it twice, then closed the binder slowly.

"Hands and feet grow first," she said. "Before arms, legs, and the rest. So shoes stop fitting before anything else does."

"Before jeans?" Denny asked.

"Before jeans, before sleeves, before everything." She looked at her brother, who was still worried about Mom saying no to new shoes. He had worn duct tape on one sole since February, and the resentment on his face whenever kids mentioned sneakers had been building for weeks. She knew that look. "Come on," she said.

They found Mom in the kitchen, and Jade laid out the notebook, the measurements, and the comparison of hands. "He'll keep growing into everything else soon," she finished. "His feet are just early." Mom sighed at the numbers, then measured Denny's foot with the wooden ruler, and drove them both to the shoe store before dinner.

At the store, Denny ran one lap around the aisle in his new shoes while Jade waited by the register, holding his old pair. "Transport these to the donation bin when we get home," Mom said, handing her the bag. In the dry, arid heat of the parking lot, Denny was still bouncing. "Your feet will be next," he told her, pointing at her pinching sneakers. Jade wiggled her toes and laughed. "Already are."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
story:
The lights went out all at once, and Ava froze in the middle of Gran's kitchen with a half-washed plate in her hands. From the living room, Gran's chair scraped the floor. "Third time this month," Gran muttered, and Ava heard her shuffle toward the hallway closet where the candles lived.

"Wait," Ava called, setting the plate down and drying her hands in the dark. She was thinking about the fire-safety unit from school in the fall. The officer had stood at the front of the room and said safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house. Ava had written it in her notes and even got the citation right on the quiz, the page number from the handbook. Now the sentence came back to her whole.

"Gran, don't light those yet." She felt her way along the counter, found the drawer, and pulled out the two flashlights Gran kept beside the batteries. The first one clicked on, a steady beam. "Flashlights are safer than candles. A candle can start a fire in a dark house." Gran paused, matchbox still in her hand, then laughed a little and put it back.

Ava carried the smaller flashlight to the front window and swept the beam across the street. Every house on the block was dark, so the problem wasn't Gran's old wiring, which Gran was always grumbling about. "It's the whole street," Ava reported. "Maybe a line came down somewhere." She found her phone, checked the power company's outage map, and saw the little shaded patch covering their neighborhood, with a repair time of two hours.

Gran declared they would sustain themselves with ice cream before it melted, and they ate it straight from the carton on the porch steps, watching a distant repair truck's lights blink through the trees. "You're a resilient one," Gran said, handing Ava the spoon. "Most people would have just sat in the dark." Ava aimed the flashlight at the sidewalk and drew a long bright line toward the road.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20.
story:
Victor had promised his best friend Dexter that they would finish their Lunar New Year poster on the same day as the big dinner at the community hall, which meant he had to know exactly when the dinner would be. "Grandma," he said, poking his head into the kitchen, "is the party on February fourth again this year?" Grandma laughed so hard she nearly dropped a dumpling. "February fourth? Last year, maybe. This year the new moon falls somewhere else."

Victor frowned at the calendar on the wall, which had red circles jumping around like startled crickets. One year the celebration landed in late January, another year in the middle of February, and once it had almost coincided with his birthday, which had made for one spectacular cake-and-dumpling double feature. He decided to test an idea. If the date moved, maybe it moved in a pattern, the way his little sister's losing streak at rock-paper-scissors followed a rule only she understood. He wrote down every date Grandma could remember, then grabbed the old calendars from the junk drawer.

His sister Mei leaned over his shoulder. "You look like a detective," she said. "A very hungry detective." He waved her off and kept sorting. The dates all sat between January 21 and February 20, and Grandma had said something about the new moon. So the rule, he figured, was this: Lunar New Year falls on a new moon, and that new moon lands somewhere inside those dates. His plan for the poster could still work, as long as Dexter agreed to build it around the dinner instead of a fixed day.

At the hall, the lion dance had just started, drums booming, and Victor found Dexter by the refreshment table, guarding the spring rolls. "Good news," Victor announced. "It's a moving target, but a predictable one. New moon, between January 21 and February 20, every single year." Dexter took a vigorous bite of a spring roll and crumbs flew like confetti. "So we make the poster a detective case," he said. "The date is the fugitive." Grandma, passing by with a tray, sniffed. "In my day we just looked at the calendar." Mei raised her cup of tea like a toast. "The fugitive will strike again next year," she said.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
Emilia's hands were shaking again, and she hadn't even opened the envelope yet. The letter from the science fair committee had been sitting on the kitchen table since Tuesday, and every time she walked past it, her stomach clenched like a fist. She had been nominated for the regional finals by her teacher, which should have felt like winning, but instead it felt like being handed a bomb with a ribbon on it.

"Still not opening it?" her brother Theo asked, sliding into the chair across from her with a bowl of cereal.

"I'm building up to it," Emilia said. "Slowly."

"Nominate you for what, disappearing contests? You've been hiding up in your room all week."

She glared at him, but he wasn't wrong. She thought about last month, before the nomination, when she'd actually liked her science project. She'd spent evenings in the garage testing water samples from the creek, laughing when Theo spilled pH solution on his shoe. Then the letter came, and something in her had switched off. Her stomach hurt. She couldn't sleep. On Friday she'd fallen asleep during math, which she never did.

That afternoon her mother drove her to the clinic because the stomachaches wouldn't quit. Dr. Okafor listened, asked questions, and ran tests that came back normal. Then she leaned forward and said, "I think your body's been running on stress too long. There's a hormone called cortisol, made by the adrenal glands, and it rises during stress. When stress lasts for weeks, cortisol can stay high, and that can leave you feeling run down." Emilia had scribbled it all in her notebook, because facts were easier to hold than feelings.

Now, sitting at the kitchen table, she opened the notebook and read her own handwriting. Her anxiety had started the day the letter arrived. It had lasted weeks. If the doctor was right, her body was still churning out cortisol like a factory that forgot to close. "Theo," she said slowly, "I have a hypothesis. The stomachaches aren't random. They follow the stress. If the stress stops, the cortisol should come down."

"So stop being stressed," Theo said, as if that were obvious.

"That's not how it works. I need coping stuff. Actual strategies." She flipped to a blank page and made a list: breathing exercises, walks by the creek, talking to Mom instead of hiding. At the bottom she wrote one more line in careful letters: I will set boundaries. No practicing past eight o'clock, and no reading the judges' comments fifty times.

She took a breath, picked up the envelope, and tore it open. "I'm in the finals," she said, and her voice came out steady. "Round one's in three weeks."

"Plenty of time," Theo said, raising his cereal spoon like a toast. "Your stress guild will just have to find a new member."

"Not everything's a guild," Emilia said, but she laughed, and her stomach, for the first time in days, stayed quiet. She taped the acceptance letter above her desk, right next to the list, and went outside to the creek with her sample kit.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen every two hours outdoors, and immediately after swimming or sweating.
story:
Jordan had been counting down to this beach trip for eleven days, and when the car finally rolled into the sandy lot by the dunes, he was out the door before Dad even killed the engine. Mom handed him the sunscreen tube at the picnic table. "Whole face, ears, back of the neck," she said, and he did it fast, because the waves were calling. That was nine in the morning.

By ten, he was bodysurfing. By eleven, he and his cousin Tessa were digging a trench so long that a jogger stopped to admire it, and the jogger's dog, a lush golden retriever named Biscuit, lay down in the hole and refused to move. Jordan was sweating from all the shoveling. Then he went straight back into the water, and Tessa followed, and they stayed in until their fingers wrinkled, then out for sandwiches, then in again. Nobody mentioned sunscreen once all day. The afternoon sun didn't feel hot in the water; it felt like nothing at all, which Jordan would later decide was the tricky part.

At four o'clock, toweling off, he caught sight of his shoulders in the truck's side mirror. They were pink. Really pink, the color of the shrimps in the cooler. Tessa's nose was peeling already at the edges. "Mom's going to make us read the sunscreen tube as punishment," Tessa groaned, and Jordan, curious now, flipped the tube over and read the back while the wind tried to snatch it.

"Reapply every two hours," he read out loud, "and immediately after swimming or sweating." He counted backward on his fingers, feeling like a detective in one of the memoirs Grandpa was always writing about his Coast Guard days. One application at nine. Swimming by ten. Sweating by eleven. Seven hours with nothing extra. The morning coating must diminish over time, or wash off, or both, and they had never once renewed it. That was the whole mystery solved in one sentence on a plastic tube. "We did everything wrong in exactly the right order," he told Tessa, and she laughed even while pressing cool fingers to her nose.

Aloe gel became the evening's main event. Dad lined them up on the porch of the rental cottage and dabbed it on while Biscuit's owner, who turned out to be staying next door, watched with amusement. Jordan held up the sunscreen tube like a trophy. "Two hours, every time," he announced. "And after swimming. Even sweating counts."

"And tomorrow?" Tessa asked, already grinning.

Jordan shook the tube. It sloshed, half full. "Timer on my watch. First one to remind me gets the last popsicle."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The Hurricanes had lost every game so far, and they had yelled at each other through all of them. Jake sat on the bench after practice, lacing and unlacing his cleats, listening to Marcus and Dev argue about who should take the free kicks. Marcus wanted to be captain so badly that he had started wearing an armband he made himself, and Dev said the armband meant nothing. The whole team had become a controversy on legs, as Jake's older sister would say.

At home, Jake dug through her old report on teamwork that she had left on the kitchen table. He had to extract the page he wanted from under a stack of her magazines. The report said that a psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Jake read the line twice. Forming was when a group first got together. Storming, the report said, was the arguing stage. Norming was when they settled things. Performing was when they finally worked. He thought about the last three weeks of the Hurricanes and felt something click, like a puzzle piece turning over in his hand.

He remembered the very first practice, back when school had just started. Nobody had known anyone's name, so they had all stood in an awkward circle passing the ball politely, saying "nice try" even after terrible passes. That was the forming part, he realized. Then the storming had begun, game by game, argument by argument.

Before the next practice, Jake texted his sister from the kitchen: Do you still have that Tuckman report? We're stuck in the storming stage and I want to know how long it lasts. She wrote back: It lasts as long as it lasts. But it doesn't last forever. Show them the report. So Jake photocopied it and brought the page to the field, where the October grass was damp and the goal nets sagged with morning dew.

He read the four words out loud while the team stretched. "Forming, storming, norming, performing," said Marcus slowly, tugging his homemade armband up his arm. "So we're not broken. We're just in the middle." Dev squinted at the page, then at Marcus. "Fine," he said. "You can call the plays. But I take the free kicks." Marcus nodded once, the way captains do in movies.

The Saturday game was still sloppy in the first half, and the goals they gave up felt like the cumulative weight of the whole season pressing down. But in the second half, when the ball came loose near midfield, Marcus shouted a play without shouting at anyone, and Dev touched it once and slid it to Jake, who was already running into the open space. Jake struck it low, toward the far post, and watched it curl inside the net. The team piled on him in the wet grass, and from somewhere under the heap of players, Marcus yelled, "That's performing, right there!"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow squeaks underfoot when it is very cold, because the hard ice crystals rub and break instead of melting slightly under pressure.
story:
Riley woke to his phone buzzing and a text from school in bright letters across the screen: closed for snow. He pressed his face to the window and saw the park across the street buried in white, the swings wearing thick snowy caps. He had promised Mrs. Okafor next door that he would check on her cat while she was away, and he had promised his friends he would meet them at the sledding hill by ten. He pulled on two pairs of socks and started out.

Halfway across the park, he noticed something odd. Every step he took made a loud squeak, like a rubber duck being stepped on. Squeak, squeak, squeak, all the way past the frozen duck pond. He stopped and pressed his boot down slowly, and the snow cried out under it. He remembered yesterday, when the snow had been soft and quiet and he had rolled it into balls without a sound. The snow had not changed color or shape. Something invisible had changed underneath it.

"The squeak means it got colder," he said out loud, to nobody. He tried an experiment. He stomped hard on a patch of snow, then stepped gently on another patch, and both times the crystals crunched and broke with the same sharp noise instead of squishing quietly like they had yesterday. Warm snow gave a little under his boot. This snow was too hard and icy for that, so it snapped and squealed instead. He looked at the sky, flat and gray, and zipped his coat all the way to his chin.

At the sledding hill, his friend Dara was taking a census of everyone who had showed up, walking around with a mitten full of pebbles and dropping one in her pocket for each kid on the hill. "Twelve," she announced, "but Marcus says thirteen, so we're counting again." Riley told them about the squeaking snow, and they all stomped in a circle like a small thunderstorm until a park volunteer asked them to settle down. They decided to nurture the half-built snow fort near the picnic tables instead, packing the squeaky snow into firm walls that rang under their mittens.

Dara wanted to sled straight down the icy slope that ended near the benches, but Riley shook his head. "That part's frozen solid now, like the squeaky snow. That's why it's squeaking. It would be reckless to hit those benches at that speed." They chose the slower hill instead, and Riley's first run was smooth and quiet, his scarf snapping behind him. At the bottom he looked back up at his boot prints, a dotted line of small dark marks, and heard Dara squeaking her way down after him, laughing the whole ride.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
The class group chat had existed for exactly one day, and it was already a mess. Norah sat at her computer lab station scrolling through the messages. Someone named SoccerStar09 had written "BE AT THE FIELD AT THREE" in all capitals, and Marcus had replied "WHY ARE YOU YELLING AT ME." Then came twenty minutes of arguing about who was angry and who was not.

"He wasn't yelling," Norah said to Priya, who sat at the next computer. "He just types in capitals. My grandpa does it too. But it reads like yelling, so everyone presumed he was mad."

"Then why does he do it?" Priya asked.

Norah clicked over to a search page. "I want to know if anyone ever wrote actual rules for this. Like, official ones." She typed "official online manners" and hit enter. The results loaded slowly, one blue link at a time. Then she found something odd: a document with a plain, number-like name.

"Look at this," she said. "It's called RFC 1855. It's one of the first written guides to online manners, and it was published in 1995."

"1995?" Priya leaned over. "That's before my parents even had the internet at home."

"Here's the title," Norah said, scrolling. "Netiquette Guidelines." She read a line out loud. "'Don't use all capitals. It looks like you're shouting.' So it's a real rule, and it's old."

Priya pointed at the screen. "You could make it our class rule and say it's official. Nobody would even know where it came from."

"That's biased," Norah said. "If I only show them the one rule about capitals, I'm picking the part that proves my point." She kept reading. The guide said to be careful in public spaces, where lots of people see what you write, and to remember that a message to one person is not the same as a message to everyone. "The chat is public. Our whole class is in it."

They printed the rule about capitals, and Norah pinned it to the corkboard by the door. By the end of the lab period, three people had come over to read it. Marcus copied it into the chat as "RULE ONE." SoccerStar09 replied with "ok ok," all lowercase, and then, a minute later, "i can't find the shift key anymore."

Norah was about to log off when a new message appeared. It was from Ms. Alvarez, their teacher, and every word was in capitals: "GREAT WORK ON THE RULES, EVERYONE."

Priya started laughing before Norah could say anything. "Go tell her."

Norah unplugged her headphones, walked to the front of the room, and held up the printed page. "Ms. Alvarez? You might want to read this."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Facing a person with hearing loss and speaking clearly helps them understand more than shouting does.
story:
Grandpa Frank arrived on Saturday with one duffel bag, a jar of his famous honey, and a hearing aid that whistled when he hugged her. Nora had been counting down the days all week. She had plans: board games, pancake mornings, a trip to the creek to look for frog eggs.

The trouble started at dinner. "Grandpa, do you want the butter?" she called from the kitchen while he sat at the table. He didn't turn around. She tried again, louder, practically shouting, and he just frowned at his plate. Mom leaned over and said something to him, and he laughed right away. Nora stared. How could Mom's quiet words work when her loud ones didn't?

She decided to diagnose the problem like a scientist, the way they did in science class. First hypothesis: Grandpa was ignoring her. That seemed plausible until she noticed he answered Mom every single time. Second hypothesis: it was about where Mom was standing. Mom always faced him. Nora ran a test in the living room. From behind him, she asked, "Is it supposed to rain?" Shouting it made him spin around, startled, and guess wrong twice. Then she walked around, looked straight at him, and said it again, clearly and at a normal volume. "Rain? Maybe tomorrow," he said instantly.

"So it's not louder, it's closer and facing you," Nora said, bouncing on the couch cushions. "From my perspective, I thought volume was everything."

"Faces carry a lot," Grandpa said, tapping his hearing aid. "And that whistling thing needs new batteries anyway. I've been guessing half the conversations in this house."

Here was the twist: all week, whenever Nora had muttered, he hadn't been ignoring her. He'd been pretending, nodding along, guessing from context, because he was embarrassed to keep asking people to repeat themselves. She'd thought he was grumpy. He'd thought she was avoiding him.

After that, it became their game. She'd catch herself yelling from the hallway, stop mid-word, sprint into the room, and plant herself in front of him. "Face-to-face squad," she announced, holding up a fist. He bumped it with his knuckles, grinning.

On Friday, her last morning with him, she flipped a pancake high, caught it, and turned to Grandpa before saying a word. "Perfect flip," he said. "Heard the sizzle, saw your face. Didn't miss a thing."

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: A minus sign placed directly before a word, with no space, removes results containing that word, so jaguar -car finds the animal instead of the car.
story:
Eve typed "jaguar" into the search bar for the third time, and for the third time the first screen was all car dealerships. Her science report was due Friday, and she needed facts about the animal, not a dealership offering zero percent financing.

Her older brother Marcus leaned over her shoulder from the couch, where he had a library copy of a notorious rocker's memoir open on his lap. He wanted to finish it before his book club meeting on Saturday, and Eve's typing was slowing down the wifi he blamed for everything.

"Everything's an ad," Eve said, pointing at the top of the page. "How do I even tell what's real?"

Marcus set the memoir face-down on the cushion. "The ones that say 'Sponsored' in the corner, they paid to be there. And anything trying to sell you a car, that's a clue." He picked the book back up. "This rock guy was notorious for throwing TVs out of hotel windows, by the way. Whole chapter on it."

Eve studied the page. The top three results had "Sponsored" labels and prices. Below them sat a zoo page, a wildlife fund page, and a page titled "Jaguar Cars Reviews." She scrolled past it and found three more car pages, then more dealerships. The animal facts were buried on page two, under a result that looked like it had been written in 2009.

She tried "jaguar animal," which helped a little, but the cars still crowded in. Then she noticed something in the search tips box at the bottom of the screen, small gray text she had skipped twice before. A minus sign placed directly before a word, with no space, removes results containing that word. She tested it, typing jaguar -car, and hit enter.

The dealerships vanished. Every result on the first screen was the animal: a fact sheet, a rainforest site, a page with a range map. Eve bookmarked three of them, then closed the laptop.

"Fixed it," she said.

Marcus held up the memoir. "This guy could never," he said, and went back to his chapter.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
Brooklyn counted the crumpled bills in her hand again at the counter of her uncle's gas station: four dollars and thirty-five cents. Last month, strawberries at the farmers' market had cost eight dollars a basket, which meant her plan for a strawberry shortcake had collapsed on the sidewalk outside the gym. Behind her, the drink cooler hummed, and Mr. Ruiz, who came every Tuesday for the same ten gallons of gas, was stacking jars of his grandmother's salsa on the counter, hoping Uncle Marco would sell them beside the chips. His salsa needed tomatoes, and good ones, and he wanted them cheap.

"Market day," Uncle Marco said, nodding at the window. The farmers' market shared the gravel lot with the station on Saturdays, and Brooklyn watched a flatbed truck roll in, then another, their beds stacked so high with strawberry baskets that the driver had to regulate his speed over the speed bump to keep them from sliding. A third truck followed. Every farmer seemed to have berries, rows and rows of red in the morning light, and the field behind the station, dark and fertile from all the June rain, had been dotted with pickers all week.

Brooklyn walked out and stood at the first stall. "How much?"

"Four dollars a basket," the farmer said. "It's the peak of the harvest season. Everybody's got the most they'll have all year."

She did the math twice. Half of eight. She tested it at the next stall anyway, and the next, and every sign said the same thing, four dollars, sometimes three fifty. She bought two baskets and still had coins left for whipped cream.

On her way back she stopped beside Mr. Ruiz. "Tomatoes are probably cheap right now too," she said. "Everything's coming in at once." He straightened up, looked at the trucks, and grinned at the baskets in her arms.

"I'll follow you," he said, and carried his empty crate toward the stalls.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.
story:
Gavin had thirty minutes before the community center spelling bee started, so he wandered into the little library off the gym, looking for a quiet corner to calm his nerves. On a bottom shelf, wedged between dusty encyclopedias, sat a fat old book with a cracked leather cover. He opened it carefully. The pages smelled like dust and rain, and the words were printed in long, narrow columns. It was a dictionary, but not like the one at school. This one looked ancient.

"Who decided how words are spelled?" he asked Priya, who had followed him in. "I mean, somebody had to. Somebody had to write down that C-A-T is cat and not K-A-T."

Priya flipped the brittle pages with one finger. "Look at the front. There might be a name." There was. A portrait of a stern man in a wig, and printing underneath that Gavin read slowly. "It says Samuel Johnson," he said. "Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled." He read the sentence twice, because it seemed like a big job for one man. "So before that, spellings were kind of loose. And this book helped pin them down."

"That's a weird thing to think about," Priya said. "Like, spelling wasn't always a rule?" Gavin tested the idea in his head, the way he tested everything. If spellings were once unsettled, then the weird silent letters he hated, the G-H in "night," must have been locked in by somebody's choice, not by magic. That made them less annoying, somehow. They were history, not tricks.

The bell rang and they hurried to the gym. Gavin sat in the second row of folding chairs and waited through three rounds. A boy named Marcus got "impulsive," spelled it wrong, and shrugged. Then the moderator called Gavin's word. "Larva," she said. Gavin pictured the old dictionary, all those settled letters, and took his time. "L-A-R-V-A. Larva." "Correct," she said.

In the final round the moderator said, "Illustrate." Gavin thought of the stern man in the wig, and of the tiny drawing of a caterpillar in the old book that had seemed to illustrate its own entry. "I-L-L-U-S-T-R-A-T-E. Illustrate." The moderator nodded, and Gavin, holding his blue ribbon, whispered to Priya, "Samuel Johnson would be proud."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
Payton slid her phone across the table so her brother Dex could see the text from Nadia. "Fine, it's wrong, but it's just my opinion that the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin." Dex read it twice, then put a piece of broccoli in his mouth and chewed for a long time, as if the broccoli might have an answer.

"That can't be right," Payton said. "If it's an opinion, nobody can check it. Like if I say broccoli tastes like old socks, you can't look that up." She pointed at his plate. "You can be indifferent to broccoli all you want, that's your opinion, and nobody can prove you wrong. But the Eiffel Tower is either in Paris or it isn't. There's one answer. It's a claim." Dex swallowed. "So?" "So it's a wrong claim, not an opinion. It's just a false one." She picked the phone back up and typed: what if I told you my opinion is that you owe me fifty dollars? That's checkable. You can check your pockets.

Dex grinned. "She's going to say that's different." "It's not different." Payton set the phone face down next to her fork, then lifted it again, then set it down again. Their dad, who had been quietly moving rice around his plate this whole time, looked up. "Is this about the France project?" "Nadia put the Eiffel Tower in the wrong city in our group slide," Payton said. "Mrs. Ruiz marked it. Nadia's saying it should count as an opinion so she doesn't lose points."

"Ah," said their dad, and went back to his rice, which seemed to be the most interesting thing at the table.

Payton typed one more message. "The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin is a claim. It can be checked, and it's false. Say you love Berlin, that's an opinion. Say the tower is there, that's just wrong." She hit send and waited, watching the three dots appear, disappear, and appear again. The reply came: "Fine. But I still say broccoli tastes like old socks."

"That part I'll allow," Payton said, and put her phone in her pocket.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Eyeglass prescriptions measure lens strength in diopters, with a minus sign for nearsightedness and a plus sign for farsightedness.
story:
The paper in Aurora's hand had a number on it, and she had read it six times since they left the parking lot. "Minus two," she said, staring at the little card. "It says minus two."

Her dad kept both hands on the wheel. The wipers ticked back and forth against a thin rain, and the windshield made everything outside look like it was underwater. He glanced over. "That's your prescription. From Dr. Okafor."

"I know where it's from." Aurora turned the card over, as if the back might say something kinder. "But why is it minus? It's like my eyes took a test and got a negative score." She imagined a big red mark on a paper, the kind her teacher wrote when something was wrong all the way through.

Her little brother, buckled in the back beside her, leaned toward the card. "Minus two. That's worse than zero."

"Nobody's at zero, dummy." But his words landed anyway, and she watched the raindrops slide down the window while she thought. The card listed other things too. There was a word on it, diopters, next to the numbers, and next to that, in the corner, the name of the clinic, which her mom always called the most prestigious one in three counties, the place people drove an hour to reach.

At the stoplight, her dad pivoted in his seat to face her. "You know your cousin Theo wears glasses."

"So?"

"His card says plus something. Plus three, I think. He's farsighted. You're nearsighted, near the opposite. So your numbers go the other way."

Aurora watched the light, red, then green. Her thoughts seemed to revolve around the little minus sign, going round and round it like the cars around the fountain in the town square. Minus for nearsighted. Plus for farsighted. It wasn't a grade at all. It was a direction, like east and west.

"Wait," Theo said slowly. "So a minus doesn't mean bad? It just means which kind?"

"That's what it means," her dad said, and turned back to the road.

The lens strength in diopters, minus two, sat on the card like a small answer instead of a small punishment. Aurora folded the paper along its crease and put it in her jacket pocket, the pocket with the zipper, where important things went.

The glasses would be ready Thursday. She looked out at the rain, at the streetlights she had always thought were fuzzy on purpose, soft glowing blobs that everyone saw the same way. Maybe they weren't. Maybe everyone else had been reading signs and counting leaves all along, and now it was her turn.

"Can we pick the purple frames?" she asked.

"Purple frames," her dad said, and signaled the turn for home.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In farsightedness, light focuses behind the retina, so near objects look blurry, and it is corrected with convex lenses.
story:
"Read the smallest line you can," said Nurse Okafor, pointing at the chart, and Rebecca squinted until the letters turned into gray ants marching across the wall.

Her best friend Maya sat on the cot beside her, swinging her legs. Maya had glasses already, and her eyes behind the lenses looked huge, like a cartoon owl's. Rebecca had appoint... no, she had been told to report here three times this week, ever since she'd copied the wrong homework from the board and turned in math about volcanoes.

"You'll get glasses," Maya said. "Then we can be twins. Sort of."

Nurse Okafor flipped lenses into a strange pair of frames, one at a time. "Better? Worse?" Rebecca peered through them at a poster on the near wall. Then, suddenly, the words snapped into focus so sharply she gasped.

"That one! That one's it!"

The nurse wrote a note. "You're nearsighted. Light focuses in front of your retina instead of on it, so far things blur. We fix it with concave lenses, the opposite of Maya's."

"Opposite?" Rebecca grabbed Maya's glasses and held them up next to her trial pair. Maya's lenses bulged outward in the middle, fat like lentils. Hers curved inward, thin in the middle. She looked through Maya's lens at the poster: the words shrank. Through her own: the words grew.

"Yours are convex," Maya said. "Mine are for farsightedness. Light focuses behind my retina, so near things blur."

"So that's why your eyes look gigantic and mine will look tiny!" Rebecca turned to the mirror and laughed out loud. The trial frames made her eyes look like two little buttons.

"Twins, huh," said Maya.

"Opposite twins." Rebecca skipped to the door, then stopped. "Wait. What if I hold your glasses inside mine? Would they cancel out and make everything neutral?"

"Only one way to find out," said Maya, holding out the glasses.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow looks white because its many clear ice crystals scatter and reflect all colors of light in every direction.
story:
The snow started before sunrise, and by seven o'clock the school website flashed the words Nathan had been hoping for all winter: CLOSED. He whooped so loudly that his mother sent him outside before he woke the whole house. At the end of the driveway he ran straight into Mrs. Okoye, who was out with her shovel. "Perfect timing," she said. "I'll pay you in hot chocolate if you clear my walk."

Nathan shoveled fast, but halfway through he stopped and stared at her birdbath. It had frozen solid, and the ice was glassy and clear as a window. Yet her whole yard, made of the same frozen water, glowed pure white. That made no sense at all. He picked up a chunk of birdbath ice and held it beside a mittful of snow, turning both over and over.

"Here's my idea," he announced, because an idea felt too big to keep quiet. "It's not about what the ice is made of. It's about how many pieces it's in." Mrs. Okoye raised an eyebrow, so he emphasized each word by rapping the ice chunk with his knuckle. "One big piece, you can see through it. A million tiny pieces? Maybe not." He carried the chunk to the driveway and smashed it with the back of the shovel, once, twice, three times, until it crumbled into a pile of glittering crumbs. He scooped them up and looked. White. Completely, unmistakably white, and when he pressed them together in his palm they caught the light and sparkled just like snow. "The crystals are still clear," he said, holding one crumb up to the sun so Mrs. Okoye could see through it. "But all those little clear pieces must scatter light and reflect every color in every direction, and all the colors together look white. That's the whole yard!"

Inside, she poured the hot chocolate and let him set a crumb of ice on the warm radiator to watch it melt. "Careful, don't touch," she warned, nodding at the space heater in the corner. "That old thing is flammable near the curtains, so we keep our distance." Nathan didn't mind. Any leftover resentment he had about shoveling had melted faster than the ice. He pressed his nose to the window and watched the falling flakes. "Millions of tiny mirrors," he said. "Every single one of them."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
story:
The cast on Kate's left arm itched in a place she could not reach, which she decided was the second worst thing about the emergency room. The worst thing was waiting for the doctor to come back with her X-ray. When he finally clipped the film onto the light box on the wall, she forgot about the itch entirely. Her bones glowed white against a gray fog, like ghosts of sticks, and one of them near her wrist had a dark crack running through it.

"Why are the bones white when everything else is basically invisible?" she asked.

The doctor was already halfway out the door, called away to supervise a new patient arriving by ambulance, so he only said, "Calcium," and vanished behind the curtain. Kate frowned at the word. Calcium, like in milk commercials. She stared at the film and turned the clue over in her mind. Calcium must be the reason bones looked different, but that still did not tell her why different meant white instead of gray.

In the next bed, behind a thin blue curtain, a boy was getting a cut on his chin checked. Kate heard his mom say something about a laser pointer, that her son had been waving a counterfeit one, a cheap knockoff from the fair, and that was how the whole fight with his brother had started. Kate was not really listening. She was thinking about light. The X-ray machine shot something through her arm, and whatever it was, some of it got through and some did not, or the picture would not show anything at all. So the white parts must be where the beam stopped. If calcium made bones white, then calcium had to be soaking up the rays, more of them than her skin and muscle did, because those parts showed up as barely-there gray.

She tested her idea against the picture itself. The crack in her bone was darker, almost the gray of the soft tissue. If the calcium was doing the blocking, then a crack meant less calcium in that spot, less blocking, and the gray showing through like a window. The dark line and the white bone fit together like a lock and a key.

"So it's calcium," she said when the doctor came back. "The calcium soaks up more of the X-rays than the soft stuff around it, so the bones print white."

"That's it exactly," he said, and pulled out a marker. "Want me to sign your cast where the break is? I can draw the crack for you."

"Draw it dark," Kate said, holding out her arm. "Like on the film."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
Muhammad slid into his usual seat on the bus, third row from the back, and pulled out his phone. The group chat for the science fair team was blinking with new messages. He read the first one and his stomach dropped. Someone had written, about Theo, the new kid who had joined the team on Monday, "Why did we let the weird kid in? He'll just ruin everything." The name on the message was Dylan.

That was the part Muhammad couldn't make fit. Dylan sat two rows ahead of him on this exact bus every morning. Dylan was the kid who held the door for substitute teachers, who said "excuse me" to kindergartners, who had once carried Muhammad's dropped binder half a mile down the hallway to return it. Muhammad leaned forward and watched Dylan laugh quietly at something his seatmate said, polite even in his laughter. In person and on the screen, it was like two different people.

The chat's whole purpose was to organize the project, and if Theo got pushed out now, he would be excluded from the team without ever knowing why. Muhammad wanted to fix it before first period. He typed a reply, deleted it, and tried another. Words on a screen felt different from words in the air, heavier somehow, and easier to throw. He thought about his older cousin Amir, who had told him last summer, "People say stuff online they'd never say to your face. Psychologists call it the online disinhibition effect." Muhammad hadn't believed it mattered much. Now he wondered.

He decided to test it. Instead of typing, he stood up, wobbling with the bus around the curve by the park, and dropped into the empty seat beside Dylan. "Did you write that about Theo?" Muhammad asked, keeping his voice low so the whole bus wouldn't hear.

Dylan's face went pale. "It was supposed to be a joke," he mumbled. "Just for the chat. I didn't think he'd see it."

"He's in the chat, Dylan. He's going to see it."

Dylan stared at his shoes for a long moment. Then he took out his phone, typed fast, and held the screen up so Muhammad could read it. "I'm sorry, that was out of line. Theo, you're on the team and I'm glad." He added a second message before Muhammad could speak. "New amendment to the chat: no writing anything we wouldn't say out loud on the bus."

"That's a good rule," Muhammad said. "Same as in real life."

"It is real life," Dylan said, and waved at Theo, who was climbing on at the next stop, backpack straps dangling. Dylan scooted over and patted the empty seat beside him.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
At dinner Aria kept her phone face down beside her plate, and she kept glancing at it anyway. Her brother Marco was talking about the garage again. "If we renovate it, I could have a place for my models," he said, spooning noodles onto his plate. "There's room for a workbench and everything. I already measured." Dad nodded, chewing. "We'd have to clear out the paint cans first. Old paint is flammable, so it can't sit near the heater." Marco said he'd carry every can to the curb himself if it meant the garage became his workshop by summer.

Aria wasn't really listening. Her stomach had been tight since lunch, when Priya had grabbed her phone off the cafeteria table and read her messages out loud, laughing. "You'd like it if you weren't so serious," Priya had said, scrolling. Aria had frozen, the way she always did, and afterward her hands shook for a whole period. She thought about it now, turning her fork in the pasta. Why did she never say anything until it was too late? She noticed a pattern: with most people she spoke right up, but with Priya she went quiet, and the tight-stomach feeling, the one her counselor called anxiety, always followed.

"Everything okay over there?" Mom asked. "You've moved one noodle around your plate for five minutes." Aria took a breath and tried a small experiment, the one her counselor had suggested as a way of coping with stress. Start small. Say one true thing. "Priya went through my phone today," she said. "Without asking."

Marco put down his fork. "That's why you were weird at lunch." Mom asked what Aria had done, and Aria admitted she had done nothing, and her eyes stung. "It's like she thinks my stuff is community property."

"It's not," Mom said. "You get to decide who touches your things, and how people treat you. That's yours to set." Aria turned that over. A boundary, she thought, was exactly what Priya was missing, a line about what Aria was comfortable with, like how Dad's paint cans had a rule: nothing flammable near the heater. The rule wasn't mean. It just kept things from catching fire.

"But Priya's my best friend," Aria said. "What if she gets mad?"

"So she gets mad," Marco said. "If I can survive Dad saying maybe to the garage, you can survive Priya being mad for a day." He was already sketching the workbench on a napkin, undeterred, planning like the garage was certain.

After dinner, Aria picked up her phone and typed: Can we talk tomorrow? It's important. Then she cleared her plate and set it in the sink.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
story:
Dylan's stomach did a happy flip when he spotted the lanterns strung over the park gates, red and gold and swinging in the breeze like they were waving him in. The cultural festival had food stalls, a drum team warming up, and, most important, a gift booth where he needed to make a big decision. His dad's colleague, Mr. Chen, had just bought a new house, and the whole family was invited to the housewarming on Saturday. Dylan had twenty dollars of allowance burning in his pocket, and he was determined to pick the gift himself.

At the booth, a wall of possibilities generated instant panic. Painted bowls, tea sets, a lucky bamboo plant, and, right at eye level, a gorgeous cherry-red wall clock with a brass pendulum. It chimed on the hour, the vendor demonstrated, and Dylan could already picture it ticking above Mr. Chen's fireplace. "Perfect," he said out loud. "Everyone needs to know the time."

He was reaching for his money when he noticed the vendor's smile flicker, just for a second, the way his gym teacher's did when someone picked teams badly. Odd. The vendor hadn't said no, hadn't said anything. Dylan tested a hunch. "Would your family hang this clock in a new house?" he asked.

The vendor shook her head, still polite, and called over a girl about Dylan's age who was stacking boxes behind the stall. "My daughter will explain better than me." The girl wiped her hands on her jeans. "In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death." She shrugged, like it was no big deal, but Dylan's ears went hot. He had almost marched into a housewarming carrying the world's worst present.

"Okay," he said slowly, working it through. "So the clock is out. But a clock and a bowl and a plant are all just objects. The problem isn't the thing, it's what the thing sounds like when you give it." The girl grinned. "Now you're getting it. Nobody's immune to a awkward gift, trust me. I once gave my grandma a white umbrella." Dylan decided not to ask. He bought the lucky bamboo instead, and the girl wrapped it in red paper with a looped ribbon, showing him how to hand it over with both hands because one hand was for strangers.

At the Chen house on Saturday, the smell of sesame oil and steamed dumplings rolled out the front door. Mr. Chen bowed slightly, and Dylan, remembering the girl's quick lesson, bowed back, a little too deep so his nose nearly hit the gift. He offered the bamboo with both hands. Mr. Chen's whole face opened up like a lantern lighting. "Ah! Lucky bamboo! Dylan, you are welcome at our table anytime." At dinner Dylan copied everyone, waiting until the eldest guest lifted his chopsticks first, and when Mrs. Chen slid the last dumpling onto his plate, he said the one Chinese phrase the girl had drilled into him outside the gates. "Xièxie." Mrs. Chen laughed and refilled his tea to the brim.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
Cole had come to Maya's house to help her family get ready for the neighborhood cultural festival, and he had been folding flyers for forty minutes when Maya held up the banner and frowned. "Grandpa painted this word across the top and I can't tell if it's even spelled right," she said. The banner showed a map of islands strung like beads across an ocean, with the word DIASPORA in tall blue letters above it.

"My cousin thinks it means 'parade,'" said Maya's little brother Theo, who was supposed to be carrying boxes but was mostly evading them, sliding behind the couch whenever a box came near. "Tell him it's not parade," Maya said. "Grandpa drives up at noon and he'll want it displayed at the table, and if someone asks me what it means, I'll just stand there sweating." Cole looked at the word again. He said it out loud twice. It sounded Greek to him, the kind of word that ended in an "a" because it had traveled a long way through other languages. He had an idea about that but no proof, and he didn't want to guess wrong in front of a whole festival.

"Your grandpa's phone number is on the fridge, right?" Cole asked. Maya said he was driving and couldn't talk. So Cole tried the stack of books Grandpa had left beside the banner, a dictionary so old its cover felt like cloth. He ran his finger down the D's while Theo, finally useful, held the page flat. "Here," Cole said, and read silently first, because he wanted to be sure before he said anything out loud.

"Diaspora," Cole read. "It comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors." Maya looked at the banner's map, then at the beads of islands, then at the photo taped to the table of Grandpa's village on one of those islands. "So the banner is saying, here's where we started, and here's us now, everywhere," she said. "That's actually kind of beautiful. And I can tell people at the table, instead of just pointing at snacks." Theo said, "I still think parade is a better word for a festival," and Maya told him he was an exceptional nuisance, but she said it while handing him a cookie, so he took it as a compliment.

At the festival, a woman with a lanyard stopped at their table and asked about the banner, and Maya answered without sweating at all. Cole stood nearby arranging flyers and feeling quietly pleased, since his dictionary guess had held up. Later, during a slow stretch when the crowd drifted toward the food trucks, Maya and Cole sat behind the table in the shade, sharing a bag of chips at their leisure, watching people wander past the banner. A girl about their age stopped, pointed at the word, and said, "What's that mean?" Maya smiled and opened her mouth, and Cole leaned back to listen to her get it exactly right.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, if the door stays closed.
story:
The candles on the coffee table made everyone look like they had three shadows each, which Joseph decided was the best thing about the power cut so far. The worst thing was that his little sister, Maya, had already eaten the emergency snacks by five o'clock. Now it was almost bedtime, dark, and warm in a way the house never usually was, because the fridge and freezer had stopped their quiet humming.

Joseph wandered into the kitchen for no reason except that wandering was something to do. He touched the freezer door out of habit, then stopped himself with his hand still on the handle. Mom had said that morning, "No opening it, whatever you do," but she hadn't said why, and Joseph liked knowing why.

"Dad," he called into the living room, "how long can the food in there survive?"

Dad appeared in the doorway, holding a candle that dripped wax onto his slipper. He didn't know, which Joseph found shocking. Dad knew how to generate electricity with a car battery and knew which birds in his book were migratory, but this, apparently, was a mystery. "We could ask the internet," Dad said, then laughed at himself. "Except the router is as dead as the lights."

So Joseph did the next best thing. He found Mom's phone, which still had some charge, and typed the question with his thumb, squinting at the small glowing screen in the dark. The answer came up, and he read it aloud like a news announcement. "A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power. A half-full one only lasts about 24 hours, if the door stays closed."

There was a pause while everyone did the math at different speeds. "Wait," Maya said slowly. "Is ours full or half full?"

That was the real question, and Joseph couldn't answer it without opening the freezer, which would ruin everything. He sat down on the kitchen floor and thought. They had gone shopping two weeks ago. He remembered eating the last frozen pizza on Tuesday, and the fish sticks before that, and Mom saying they'd restock after payday. Piece by piece, he counted backward in his head. "We're half full," he announced. "Maybe less. Which means we've got about one day, not two."

"Then tomorrow morning, before school, we have a frozen feast," Dad said. "Fish popsicles for breakfast."

"Ew," said Maya, delighted.

Joseph marked the deadline in his mind like a line drawn on the kitchen floor. Then he took one of the candles and set it on the counter where he'd see it first thing tomorrow, right beside the freezer door.

"Guarding the treasure?" Maya asked.

"Guarding the clock," Joseph said, and blew it out.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
story:
The first dinner at Camp Winnowick was lasagna, and Colton pushed his fork through it without eating. He had written a note that morning and slipped it under the syrup dispenser in the dining hall. The note said, "If you miss home, meet me here after lunch." He had a plan: he would count who came, and that would tell him something.

At breakfast on day two, he counted four kids who looked like him, which is to say kids who talked less than they had on the bus. The loud ones, like a boy named Dax from Cabin 6, seemed fine. Colton made a chart in his notebook. His idea was that homesickness was rare, maybe one camper in ten, and he was probably one of the unlucky ones.

After lunch, he checked the syrup dispenser. His note was gone. In its place was another note, in different handwriting: "Who wants to know?" Colton sat down at the nearest table and waited, watching the door.

Dax walked in.

"You wrote the note?" Colton asked.

"Maybe you wrote it," Dax said. He sat down across from Colton and folded his arms. "Fine. Yes. I miss my mom. Don't tell anyone, I have a reputation."

Colton stared at him. "You seem like the least homesick person here."

"That's the trick," Dax said. "Nobody looks homesick."

They moved the experiment to dinner. While a counselor walked around refilling water pitchers, Dax leaned across the table and said, loudly enough for the whole bench to hear, "My little sister cried on the bus. Not me, though. Anyway, raise your hand if you miss home."

Colton held his breath. If he was right about the rare thing, maybe two hands would go up. His own hand went up first. Then Dax's. Then a girl named Priya raised hers, then a boy with a retainer, then another, then almost the whole table. The counselor, whose name was Sam, glanced over and said, "Yeah, when they did research on kids at overnight camps, they found most campers feel at least some homesickness. For most of them it stays mild." Then he went back to pouring water, like he was reporting the weather.

"Most," Colton repeated. He wrote it in his notebook. So it was the normal thing, not the rare thing, and mild was the usual version. Priya tried to console the boy with the retainer, who had started to sniffle, but he waved her off and said, "I'm fine, it's mild, the guy just said so."

Colton took a bite of lasagna. Dax stole his garlic bread, and Colton let him.

"Same time tomorrow?" Dax asked, mouth full.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly

fact: Phishing is a scam in which someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information.
story:
Wyatt's new phone sat on his desk like it might ring at any moment, even though nobody knew the number yet. Mr. Ruiz had let the class keep their phones out for the morning lesson, and Wyatt kept sliding his closer whenever the teacher turned his back. Then the phone buzzed. A text from something called GalaxyGame Support read: "Your account will be deleted in 24 hours unless you verify your password. Reply now." Wyatt's stomach dropped. He had spent all summer building that account.

He typed his password halfway before he stopped. Something felt off. Mr. Ruiz had said that real companies never ask for your password in a message, and this was asking exactly that. Wyatt tried to diagnose the problem the way he would a broken controller: test one thing at a time. His idea was simple. If the message were real, the game's actual website would mention the deletion too. He opened the browser, logged into the official site, and found nothing but a banner announcing a new update. No warning. No deadline. Then he noticed the sender's address was a random jumble of letters, nothing like the company's name on the site.

"Mr. Ruiz," Wyatt said, raising his hand. "What's it called when someone pretends to be a company to trick you out of your password?" Mr. Ruiz nodded. "Phishing." Across the aisle, Priya leaned over. "You almost fell for that?" she asked. "On day one?" Wyatt admitted he had typed three letters of his password before stopping. Priya, who had told everyone last week that phones in class were a terrible idea, frowned at her own phone and then back at him. "Okay," she said, "maybe you're more responsible than I said." She held up her screen. "I got the same text this morning. I almost replied."

Together they showed Mr. Ruiz both messages, and he forwarded them to the front office so the school could warn other kids. Wyatt blocked the sender, then sent his mom a text of his own: "Got my first scam today. Did not give them my password. You're welcome." A minute later she replied, "Proudest I've been all year." Wyatt slid the phone into his backpack, where it stayed for the rest of class, buzzing once with her message still on the screen.
