fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Layla sat cross-legged on her bed with her tablet balanced on her knees, staring at the team list in the lobby of Cloud Racers. Her best friend Marco had typed "Okay." into the chat after she suggested they team up for the tournament, and now he had gone quiet, which was strange, because Marco never went quiet. He usually typed so much that the chat window scrolled before anyone could read it.

"Did I do something?" she typed in the private message window, which was just for the two of them. In the public lobby, where forty strangers were arguing about track picks, she kept her messages short and neutral. That was the convention. Everyone said "gg" after races and "brb" for stepping away, and nobody used full sentences, because full sentences in a lobby felt like showing up to a pool party in a snowsuit.

Marco's reply took a full minute. "you sounded mad."

Layla squinted at the screen. "About what?"

"you wrote Okay. with the dot. like my mom when she's mad."

She scrolled up and checked. She had written "Okay." Marco's last three messages had no periods at all: "ok," "sure," "fine." She scrolled further, through weeks of their chats, and saw the pattern everywhere. When Marco was happy, no dots. When Marco was annoyed, dots appeared, like little period-shaped storm clouds. She had never noticed because a period was just a period, or so she had thought.

She tested it. In the private chat she sent two versions of the same word to herself, one with the dot and one without, and looked at them side by side. "Okay." did look mad. It looked like a door closing. The undotted "okay" looked like a shrug. She revised her next message carefully, deleting the period and typing "sorry i wasnt mad, just excited about the tournament," and sent it dot-free into the world.

"oh," Marco typed back. "ok good." Three seconds later: "my sister says theres a study, 2016, binghamton university, they found texts ending with a period seem less sincere than the same ones without." Layla raised an eyebrow at the screen, wondering if he had made that up and hoping she wasn't being gullible. "look it up," Marco added, as if reading her mind. Then a lobby notification flashed: the tournament countdown had started, and their team slot would go to someone else in ninety seconds.

"race you to sign up," she typed, no period, and hit enter before the lobby could fill.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading the dough makes the gluten stronger and stretchier.
story:
Jace tied Grandma's apron around himself twice because it was built for a person with a lot more Grandma in her, and he flopped the ball of dough onto the floury counter. Tonight was his night to cook, and he had promised bread, real bread, the kind that came out of the oven crackling. He pushed the dough around for about forty seconds, decided that was plenty, and dropped it back into the bowl to rise.

An hour later he peered under the towel and frowned. The dough had puffed up, sure, but when he poked it, it tore instead of springing back. It looked like a sad, dense pillow. His little sister Nadia leaned over his elbow, sniffing.

"It smells like nothing," she reported. "Also, I want to braid it. I've been practicing on my hair, and I'm amazing now."

"You can braid it when it behaves," Jace said. He pulled off a small piece and stretched it gently. It ripped almost instantly, like wet paper. Something was missing, and it wasn't the flour or the water, because those were definitely in there. He had added water to flour, so whatever the water had done, it had already done it. The only step he had rushed was the pushing part.

He grabbed a fresh piece of dough and pushed and folded, pushed and folded, setting a timer for ten minutes because that was what Grandma's recipe card demanded in her cramped handwriting. Nadia chattered about her braiding plans, their dad wandered through in his tranquil Saturday mood and muttered something about the mortgage and the price of flour, and Jace kept going even when his arms complained. Around minute six something changed under his hands. The dough stopped ripping when he tugged it and started stretching, long and elastic, like it had opinions about being pulled and was winning.

"So that's it," he said. "The water makes something in there, and the pushing makes it stronger. The recipe card says the something is called gluten."

"Gluten," Nadia repeated solemnly, as if accepting a new member of the family. "Fine. It may be braided."

The second loaf rose tall and proud, and when Jace slashed the top it didn't collapse, it sighed. He slid it into the oven, and ten minutes later the kitchen smelled like the opposite of nothing. Nadia stood at the oven door with three slim ropes of dough already pinned to the counter.

"You have to let me braid it now," she said. "It's stretchy. I tested it. Gluten complies."

"Nobody says complies," Jace said, laughing, but he handed her a rope of dough anyway, and she got to work.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain.
story:
Sadie had been on the couch since Tuesday, buried under a quilt with a box of tissues, a mug of flat ginger ale, and a fever that came and went like a bad houseguest. Her throat felt like she had swallowed a handful of gravel. What she wanted most in the world, more than missed Halloween or the sixth-grade curriculum she was falling behind on, was for her headache to stop.

She remembered a flashback from when she was eight and had chickenpox, how she had scratched at the spots and her mother had carried her to the couch in this same living room, had even read her a chapter about kids who salvaged a shipwreck, and how a bottle of orange pills had sat on the shelf and nobody would give her one. Sadie had thought it was a punishment for scratching. Now, with her head pounding, she decided she was old enough to decide for herself. She got up, wrapped the quilt around her shoulders like a cape, and shuffled to the bathroom cabinet.

Aspirin. She tipped two white tablets into her palm and then paused, because taped inside the cabinet door was a note in her mother's handwriting: Not for Sadie during flu or chickenpox. Sadie stared at it. She was thirteen, not eight, and the flu was the flu, wasn't it? It seemed almost naive to think a couple of pills could hurt anyone. But her mother did not tape notes to doors for no reason. Sadie put the tablets back, carried the bottle to the living room, and waited by the window until the blue car pulled into the driveway.

"Mom," she said, holding it up. "Why is aspirin off-limits for me? I checked the label twice and there's nothing about age."

Her mother dropped her bag on the chair and took the bottle. "It's linked to something called Reye's syndrome," she said. "It's rare, but it's serious, and it affects the liver and the brain. Kids and teenagers shouldn't take aspirin during the flu or chickenpox." She set the bottle on the high shelf above the fridge, where it belonged. "There's ibuprofen in the cabinet, the small blue box. That one's fine."

Sadie took two blue tablets with a swallow of ginger ale and settled back under the quilt. Within an hour the pounding behind her eyes eased to a dull hum, and she salvaged the rest of the afternoon by reading the shipwreck chapter she never finished five years ago. When her mother checked on her before dinner, the bottle on the high shelf caught the last of the evening light, and Sadie raised her mug toward it like a toast.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
story:
Marcus held the box like it might go off, because in a way it would. Inside was his first phone, a birthday present from his parents, and he had carried it to Theo's house precisely so the whole thing could happen with a witness. Theo had gotten his own phone eight months ago and now moved through the world like a person who had signed some fundamental treaty with adulthood, which mostly meant he texted his mom from the kitchen to ask when dinner was.

"Open it already," Theo said, bouncing a tennis ball off the garage door.

Marcus peeled the tape slowly, remembering the last big thing he'd been trusted with, his grandfather's fishing knife, and how he'd lost it in the lake before summer ended. He decided this time he would be careful from minute one.

They set the phone up on Theo's porch, and Theo installed a flashlight app for him, "the most useful app ever invented," he said, holding it under his chin like a ghost. Then a box popped up on the screen. The flashlight app wanted permission to see Marcus's contacts. All of them.

"Why would a flashlight need my contacts?" Marcus asked. "It's a light. It shines."

Theo squinted at his own phone. "Mine asked for my microphone too. I just tapped yes. Everyone just taps yes."

Marcus did not tap yes. He sat back and tried to infer what was going on, the way his science teacher was always nagging them to do. A pattern was hiding under that little box, a rule about how phones worked. Maybe apps had to ask before they could use the camera, the microphone, or the contacts. And if they had to ask, maybe a no could happen whenever he wanted one, not just at the moment of asking.

"Where's settings?" he said, and hunted through the screens until he found a list of apps with little toggles next to them. Every app that had ever asked him anything was there, with its permissions listed like a confession. He flicked the flashlight app's contact permission off. The app kept shining. The light didn't care.

Theo leaned over his shoulder. "Wait. You can take it away later? I've been saying yes to everything since October." He scrolled his own settings and went pale. "This flashlight app has been listening to me. It has heard everything. It has heard me sing in the shower."

"You don't shower with your phone."

"It was near the bathroom."

Marcus laughed so hard he nearly dropped the new phone, then caught it, because minute one of careful was still going. He turned off Theo's microphone permission too, and they sat there in the porch light, two boys quietly rearranging the rules of their small digital kingdoms.

"My mom's going to say I should've thought of this months ago," Theo said, still scrolling. "She's going to be insufferable."

"Send her a text about it."

"I will." Theo grinned. "But not from the bathroom."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Lily felt fantastic after the first volleyball practice of the season. She had sprinted for every ball, done lunges across the whole gym floor, and jumped until the coach blew the whistle for water. On the walk home she was still buzzing, thinking that maybe this year she would finally make starting lineup instead of watching her chances dwindle as the roster got cut.

Two mornings later, she could barely climb the stairs to math class. Her thighs burned with every step, and when she lowered herself into her seat she made a sound like a deflating balloon. Her friend Priya leaned over. "You okay?"

"I don't get it," Lily whispered. "I was fine after practice. Great, even. And I didn't do anything yesterday. Why does it hurt now?"

Priya shrugged. "My arm was like that after my flu vaccine last month. Sore, but not until the next day, weirdly." She flexed her arm as if proving it.

Lily turned that over all through class. It didn't make sense that skipping a day would make things worse. Unless the soreness was on a delay, like mail that arrived late no matter what. She thought back to last season, when she'd sat out the first week with a sprained wrist and then gone to one hard practice; she'd felt fine that night and terrible two days after. She had blamed the cafeteria pizza at the time. Now she wondered.

At practice she tested her idea. She asked three teammates when they were soredest. Marisol said her shoulders ached worst the day after the spike drills, not the same evening. Jayla counted on her fingers and said it hit her hard around two days, then faded. Every answer landed somewhere between one and three days. Lily felt something click into place, a pattern she couldn't see but could map by asking.

The coach overheard them and paused her clipboard scribbling. "You girls discussing DOMS?" she asked.

"Is that what it's called?" Lily said. "Delayed onset muscle soreness?"

"That's the one." The coach went back to her lineup.

On the bench, tying her shoes, Lily weighed her next move. Last year she had quit soccer after one brutal week because the pain had seemed endless and she'd thought she was too weak for it. If she had known the soreness peaked and then faded, would she have stayed? She couldn't decide, and the question sat with her while the whistle shrieked and the team ran onto the court.

She had a plan, radical in its simplicity: schedule rest days right where the soreness would crest, then push hard again once it ebbed. Tonight she would ice her legs, stretch gently, and mark Thursday as her easy day. Lily stood, winced at her screaming thighs, and jogged toward the serve line anyway.

"You're limping!" Priya called.

"I know," Lily shouted back, and served the ball clean over the net.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
Maria stood in Priya's bedroom with one shoe on and one shoe off, staring at the invitation on the desk. The dance started in ninety minutes, and there was still time to eliminate the whole plan, text Priya that she felt sick, and stay home. She had done it before, twice, and she knew exactly how it worked.

"Stop hovering," Priya said from the closet. "You're hovering like a small worried cloud."

"I can't dance. That's the problem. Everyone will see that I can't dance."

Priya held up two shirts, then dropped them both and pulled out her phone instead. "Watch this first." She tapped the screen and handed it over. On it, a white cockatoo with a yellow crest was bobbing its head and lifting its feet to a pop song, exactly on the beat.

"That's a bird," Maria said.

"He's called Snowball. Scientists studied him in 2009. Aniruddh Patel led the whole thing, and they showed that Snowball could really move in time to the music. And here's the part that got me." She took the phone back, tapped, and started the video again at a different speed. "Watch. They changed the tempo, and he adjusted. He kept matching it."

Maria watched the bird shift its rhythm, stomping a little faster, then a little slower, following along. Something in her chest loosened, like a knot someone had finally found the end of. "A cockatoo can do this," she said slowly. "A bird with a brain the size of a walnut can find the beat."

"Exactly."

"So a person can." Maria put on the other shoe. It felt like a decision, not a shoe.

At the dance, the gym had been turned into something almost unrecognizable, with paper streamers and a fog machine that made the far wall look faintly ominous until you realized it was just the fog machine. Maria stood near the punch bowl for two songs, and suspense built in her stomach like a soda shaken and not yet opened. Then the DJ put on the same song from the video, and without letting herself think, she started to bob.

She matched the beat. Then she matched it faster when the chorus came, then slower, and she thought of Snowball lifting his yellow crest feet one at a time, and she laughed out loud. Priya appeared beside her, doing a move that could only be described as interpretive flamingo.

"You're doing it!" Priya shouted over the music.

Maria lifted one foot, then the other, perfectly on tempo. "If the bird can adjust, so can I!"

A boy from her science class gave her a thumbs up, and the fog machine sighed another cloud across the gym floor.

fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
The science lab chat was supposed to be for questions about the digestive system, so when Mr. Ortega posted "Reminder: intestine diagrams due Friday," Leah typed "Great, my favorite organ" and hit send before she thought about it. Three people replied with links about intestinal diseases. Marcus sent her a private message: "Are you okay? Do you actually have a stomach thing?" She stared at the screen. Her joke had traveled like a stone dropped in water, and every ripple had taken it literally.

She tried to clarify with a follow-up post: "I was joking, intestine diagrams are not actually my favorite." That only made it worse, because Priya asked why she would say that if she didn't mean it, and the whole chat scrolled on without her, arguing about whether Leah was being sarcastic or upset. Leah shut her laptop and watched Mr. Ortega sketch the small intestine on the whiteboard, feeling like the whole class had read a different sentence than the one she wrote.

That night she went looking for a way to fix it, and found something better. On a computer history site she read that on September 19, 1982, a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. People typing to each other back then had the exact same problem she'd had, and somebody had invented a mark for it. She read the date twice. Her problem was older than her parents. Somewhere along the way she had thought of :-) as obsolete, a thing her aunt used, but clearly it had been doing its job since 1982.

The next morning she asked Marcus to meet her at the picnic table by the gym before first period. "I found out why my joke blew up," she said, and told him about Fahlman, the message board, the smiley meant to flag jokes. "So this afternoon I'm going to post one in the chat. An apology with a :-) at the end, and then a real joke with one too, so people can see the difference." Marcus turned his water bottle in his hands. "Or you could just say it was a joke in plain words." He had a point, and she sat with it for a second, remembering how her plain words had already failed once.

"Both," she decided. "Words first, smiley as backup." Fifth period, she typed her apology, added :-) and watched Priya reply with a laughing face instead of a question. Marcus leaned over from the next desk and typed, "Told you it was a joke," and Leah smiled at the little sideways grin sitting at the end of her sentence, still working after all these years.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from their food every day.
story:
Alexander carried the cardboard box across the backyard with both hands, walking like someone balancing a full glass of water. Inside, under a flap of hay, sat a brown and white guinea pig named Biscuit, his first pet ever. His little sister Priya trotted beside him, already arguing that she should be allowed to hold Biscuit first because she had a special way of sitting very still.

"Biscuit is my obligation," Alexander told her, setting the box down by the new hutch under the maple tree. "That means I'm the one who takes care of him." Priya pouted, but she had her own plan. She wanted Biscuit to learn to eat from her hand so he would like her best, and she planned to sit by the hutch every single afternoon until it happened.

For the first week Alexander did what the pet store had said. He filled the bowl with dry pellets every morning and changed the water. The pellets smelled faintly sweet, like toast, and Biscuit crunched them happily enough. Then, on Saturday, Alexander noticed something odd. Biscuit was sitting in the corner of the hutch with his fur puffed up, and he didn't come to the front when Alexander rattled the bag. His eyes looked watery, and he had left his favorite tunnel untouched.

Alexander sat on the grass and thought. What had changed? Nothing, except the food, and the food had been exactly the same all week. He turned the pellet bag over and read the tiny print on the back, squinting in the sun. There it was: a line about added vitamin C. He went inside and searched on the family computer, and what he found made him sit up straight. "They can't make their own vitamin C, like humans, so they need it in their food every day," he read aloud to Priya, who had followed him in. Every day. The pellets had some in them, but Alexander remembered something else from the search, that the vitamin faded from stored feed over time, and their bag had been sitting on a shelf for who knew how long.

So he tested it. He cut a strip of red bell pepper, which the website said was packed with vitamin C, and brought it out to the hutch along with a slice of orange, wondering which one Biscuit would choose. The pepper smelled sharp and green in the cool morning air. Biscuit sniffed it, then snatched it and chewed so fast that crumbs of pepper flew onto the cedar shavings. He ignored the orange completely.

Alexander gave him fresh pepper every day after that, and within a week Biscuit's fur lay smooth again and he raced to the front of the hutch whenever Alexander's sneakers appeared on the grass. He wasn't just fine now; he seemed to thrive, popcorning straight up in the air when the food bowl rattled. Priya got her wish too, though not the way she expected. Biscuit decided the best place to eat his pepper strip was directly from her hand, and she sat by the maple tree every afternoon, giggling as his whiskers tickled her fingers. "He likes me best," she announced, and Biscuit, mouth full, made no argument.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
story:
Matthew set the stiff brushes on the kitchen table like evidence at a trial. There were five of them, and every one stood up straight, hard as popsicle sticks. He had left them in the studio overnight, and now his poster for history class sat half-finished beside them: a painted diagram of the monarchy, with a king at the top and arrows pointing down to the lords, then the knights, then the peasants crowded along the bottom.

His sister Priya wandered in and picked one up. "It's like a tiny spear," she said, poking his arm with it. "Ow. It actually hurts."

"Put it down. I have to fix them before Mom gets home or she'll say my whole art kit is obsolete." He filled a cup with warm water and dropped the brushes in. His first draft of the poster had taught him something already: when the paint was wet, a splash of water thinned it right out, and he could swirl it around, lighten a color, rinse it clean. So maybe water could rescue the brushes too. He stirred the cup and watched.

Nothing happened. The bristles stayed bent and stiff, like a hedgehog that refused to be friends with anyone. He pressed one against the rim of the cup. The water beaded off it.

"Huh," he said. He fetched a fresh brush, the one good one he'd washed properly last night, and dipped it into his red paint. Then he held it under the tap. The paint dissolved in a pink cloud and swirled down the drain. Same paint, same water. The only difference was that on the ruined brushes, the paint had dried.

"So wet paint washes out," Priya said, leaning over his shoulder, "and dry paint just... stays."

"Forever, probably. Or until I'm thirty." He remembered leaving those brushes on the studio counter, telling himself he'd clean them in the morning, and how easy that had felt at ten o'clock at night. He wondered whether it was worth asking Mom to buy new ones, or whether he'd rather accept the punishment of painting his peasants with a cotton swab. The poster still needed a border, and the peasants were all supposed to be brown, and now he owned exactly one working brush.

He swirled the good brush in the water cup, dried it on a paper towel, and dipped it into the brown. "Rule for the rest of my life," he said. "Wash the brush before it dries."

Priya held up the stiffest one. "Spear number two?"

"Fine. But aim at the trash can."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
Rosalie pulled the laptop closer and typed her cousin Marcus's favorite player into the search bar, because the argument was still running from dinner and she intended to win it. "Told you," Marcus had said, pointing at the batting average on his phone. "Point two sixty. That's not a great hitter." Her grandpa had hummed at that, the way he did when he knew something, and Rosalie had spent the whole car ride home wondering what the hum meant.

The player page loaded, all numbers stacked in tidy columns. She scrolled past the average to the row of walks, and there it was: a lot of walks, more than half the hits. She clicked to another player, one with a higher average, and counted his walks too. Far fewer. She sat back. "Huh," she said to the empty kitchen, which felt less silly than saying it to nobody at all.

She texted Marcus: come over. He lived two streets away, and luckily his free evening happened to coincide with hers, because otherwise she'd have had to explain it all in messages and he never read long messages. He arrived still holding his phone, still sure of himself.

"Look," she said, spinning the laptop toward him. "Watch what I did." She pulled up both players side by side. "Count these. Hits, and then walks." Marcus counted, lips moving. "So?" he said. "A walk isn't a hit."

"A walk isn't a hit, but it's not nothing either," Rosalie said. "Here's the thing. A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats. And walks don't count as at-bats. So the number gives a batter no credit for walks. Your guy's average looks small because the walks are invisible."

Marcus leaned in, scrolling, checking. He found a third player with a fat average and only a handful of walks all season. "Okay," he admitted, "so the average is squashing everything down to one number and it drops stuff on the floor."

Rosalie thought about the settlement they'd made last summer, when Marcus had traded her his window seat on the trip to the lake in exchange for her last two pieces of licorice, and how she'd regretted it within an hour. Numbers could be like that too, she figured. You agreed to them because they looked simple, and then you found out what they left out. "So your player's underrated," she said. "You were right for the wrong reason."

"That still counts as right," Marcus said, and he pulled the laptop back toward himself, already typing the player's name into a new search. "Grandpa's going to be endangered when I tell him he started this." Rosalie laughed and slid her chair over next to him.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
story:
Justin slid the guitar case onto the table in Ms. Reyes's studio and popped the latches like he was opening treasure. One week of lessons, and he already knew three chords, though his fingertips knew something else entirely.

"I'm not quitting," he announced, "but I have to tell you, my fingers feel like I pressed them against a hot stove. Is my guitar broken? Maybe the strings are too tight."

Ms. Reyes set down her coffee. "Play me a G chord."

He pressed down. Even before he strummed, he winced. The tips of his left hand were pink and shiny, and yesterday they had stung through his pencil in math class. He strummed anyway, because quitting before the chord was not an option.

Ms. Reyes held out her own left hand, palm up. "Feel the fingertips."

They were hard, like small pebbles under the skin. "Whoa. What happened to your fingers?"

"Calluses," she said. "Want to know the funny part?"

Justin was already piecing it together, his mind turning on some hidden pivot, the way it did when a math problem suddenly swung from impossible to obvious. "You practice a lot, right? And I've practiced every day for a week, and my fingers are sore. So the soreness comes first, and then..." He stopped, ideas germinating faster than he could line them up. "Then the skin gets tougher, and it stops hurting?"

"Play a chord on my guitar and see how the strings feel."

He took her guitar and pressed a G. His sore fingers ached, but the strings felt different, lighter somehow. "Wait, is your guitar easier?"

"It's not the guitar," she said, grinning.

Justin sat back. If the pain was inevitable for every new player, then it wasn't a sign something was wrong. It was a sign something was starting. "So everybody who ever got good at this went through exactly this week?"

She nodded. He looked down at his pink fingertips and felt like he was holding tickets to something huge. "Then I'm keeping the schedule. Every single day."

For the rest of the lesson he hammered through chord changes, counting them like push-ups, and by the last one he laughed out loud at the sting.

"Same time next week?" Ms. Reyes asked.

"Same time next week," Justin said, and he pressed one fingertip to his thumb, testing it like a tiny promise.

fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
story:
The waiting room clock said 3:40, and soccer tryouts started at 4:30, which gave Jaxon exactly fifty minutes to get the orange cast off his left arm, sign out, and ride his bike across town. He had broken the arm six weeks ago falling off the dock at his uncle's lake house, and ever since then the cast had been the rudder of his whole summer, steering every plan toward "sorry, I can't." Today the rudder came off.

In the exam room, Nurse Diaz rolled a cart toward him with something that looked like a small circular saw. Jaxon's stomach dropped. "Whoa, whoa. That thing spins?"

"That's what I thought too," Jaxon said quickly, before the nurse could answer. He sat up straighter, because he had figured this out at his last appointment and it was worth sharing. "It doesn't spin. The blade vibrates, back and forth, super fast. It cuts through the hard stuff, the plaster and fiberglass, but it won't cut your skin underneath."

The kid stopped chewing his gum. "That's impossible."

"Watch," Jaxon said. His own heart was still hammering from the memory of six weeks ago, when he had gripped the armrest so hard the nurse couldn't excavate his fingers from it, not even with both hands. The flashback made him grin now, though it hadn't been funny then. He held out his casted arm like a man volunteering for a magic trick. "Go ahead. I'll prove it."

The saw whined like an angry hornet, and Jaxon kept his eyes open the whole time. The blade buzzed down one side of the cast, then the other, a line of dust puffing out like a tiny snowstorm. When it was done, Nurse Diaz spread the halves apart with what looked like shoe horns, and there was his arm, pale and skinny and completely whole.

"See?" Jaxon said to the kid in the doorway, holding up his arm like a trophy. "Hard cast, soft skin. Back and forth, not spinning."

The kid looked at Jaxon, then at the saw, then at Jaxon again, and let out a long breath. "Okay," he said, and sat down in the chair like a normal person instead of a person planning an escape.

Jaxon signed out at 4:05, flexing his free arm in the parking lot. Twenty-five minutes. His bike waited by the rack, front wheel tipped to one side, chain guard glinting in the sun.

"Race you to tryouts," he said to nobody, and took off down the sidewalk.

knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
The Cougars had lost seven road games in a row, and Vincent had started keeping notes in the back of his math binder about it. "We stink everywhere," said Marcus, dropping his bat bag on the bench, "but especially in other people's dugouts." Vincent flipped to a fresh page and wrote Saturday, HOME, then underlined it twice, because today the Cougars were finally playing at Maple Field, their own diamond, with their own ratty net behind home plate and their own crackly scoreboard.

First inning, Marcus robbed a line drive at shortstop. Third inning, their pitcher, Dev, struck out the side. By the fifth, the Cougars were up 4-1, and Vincent felt something weird bubbling up, a feeling he had almost forgotten existed while wearing this uniform. "We're good?" he asked the bench, like he was announcing a scientific discovery. "We're actually good?"

Then it hit him, standing there in the seventh inning with the tying run on second base. It wasn't luck. His notes proved it. Every single away game, ugly loss. Every home game this season, a win. Three straight at home now, if they held on. He turned to Coach Ruiz's nephew, Benny, who kept score and knew everything about baseball. "Benny. Is there a thing where teams win more at their own park?"

Benny didn't even look up from his scorebook. "Home advantage," he said. "Home teams win more than half their games on average. Across a lot of sports, not just baseball."

Vincent's jaw dropped. It was a rule. An invisible, actual rule of the universe, and he had found it with a binder and a bad season. He wanted to test it. If home advantage was real, then the other team's batter, this scary kid named Trevor who had already homered twice in away games against them, should be easier to handle right here. So Vincent, catching, called for a low curveball, a pitch Trevor had hammered on the road. Sure enough, Trevor's swing was late by a hair, and the ball popped up into the gray sky. Marcus caught it. Inning over.

"Your testimony as scorekeeper," Vincent said grandly in the handshake line, "will confirm my theory." Benny rolled his eyes. "It's a scoreboard, not a courtroom. We won 4-2." Marcus put an arm around both of them. "So all we have to do is never leave Maple Field again. I'll write a letter."

In the parking lot, Vincent flipped open his binder one more time and wrote home advantage, big and dark, then drew a box around it. His mom honked from the car. He shoved the binder in his bag, grabbed his bat, and sprinted across the diamond yelling, "Next home game, I'm testing whether it works twice!"

fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
story:
The X-ray photos glowed on the light box, and Abigail leaned forward in her plastic chair, staring at the pale gray bone running down her forearm. Dr. Patel tapped it with a pen.

"Good news," he said. "It's a greenstick fracture."

"A what?" Abigail asked. Her mother was still filling out forms at the counter, so nobody answered for her.

"You can read about it on this sheet," the doctor said, handing her a printout, and then he went to check on another patient.

Abigail read the page twice. The bone had cracked on one side and bent on the other, like a young green branch that snaps partway through but stays connected. It happened mostly in children, because children's bones were more flexible. She looked at the X-ray again. Sure enough, one edge of the bone showed a dark jagged line, and the opposite side curved inward, like it had folded instead of snapped. So her arm was only partly broken. That was strange to think about, like being only partly asleep.

She tried to remember the fall. She had been racing Danny up the hill behind the school, the day after her mother had told her, twice, to slow down and stop showing off. She had shown off anyway. When her feet slipped on the gravel, she had thrown her right arm out to catch herself, and her whole weight had come down on it from one direction. Now that she studied the picture, the crack was on the side that would have been squeezed, and the bend was on the stretched side, exactly the way a branch bends when you push it too far. She felt a small flash of insight: the ground had pushed, and the bone had answered by cracking on one side and folding on the other. Her bones had bent because they were still young, and somehow that made the whole thing less embarrassing, not more. Still, she wondered whether she would have taken the hill slower if her mother hadn't warned her. Maybe the warning was what made her want to go faster. She couldn't decide.

Dr. Patel came back with a bucket of wet casting material and asked her to pick a color. Abigail pointed at the bright orange one, hoping to salvage something good out of a rotten week. The wrap was cool and then warm, like molten wax hardening around her arm, and she held still while it set.

"Can I still write with my left hand?" she asked.

"You'll have to," he said. "For six weeks."

Abigail looked at the orange cast, then at the X-ray still glowing on the box, at the crack and the bend in the branch of her own bone. "Fine," she said. "But Danny has to carry my backpack."
